claim: The adaptive immune system responds to pathogens by selecting clones of cells with specific receptors.
source: The adaptive immune system responds to pathogens by selecting clones of cells with specific receptors.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about adaptive immunity.

claim: The human body contains approximately 10^12 T cells.
source: Their interplay balances the breadth and specificity of the ~1012 T cells in the human body (Figure 1A; Arstila et al., 1999; Farber et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Arstila et al., 1999; Farber et al., 2014).

claim: Early estimates of TCR diversity ranged around 10^15 different possible receptors.
source: The genetic recombination of the T cell receptor (TCR) locus, termed VDJ recombination, generates an enormous potential diversity of receptors ranging from early estimates of ~1015 (Davis and Bjorkman, 1988) to more recent estimates of ~1061 (Mora and Walczak, 2016) different possible receptor TCRαβ heterodimers.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davis and Bjorkman, 1988.

claim: More recent estimates of TCR diversity are approximately 10^61 different possible receptor TCRαβ heterodimers.
source: The genetic recombination of the T cell receptor (TCR) locus, termed VDJ recombination, generates an enormous potential diversity of receptors ranging from early estimates of ~1015 (Davis and Bjorkman, 1988) to more recent estimates of ~1061 (Mora and Walczak, 2016) different possible receptor TCRαβ heterodimers.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mora and Walczak, 2016.

claim: Clonal selection expands the number of specific cells during an infection for effector functions.
source: Clonal selection expands the number of specific cells during an infection for effector functions, a fraction of which is retained over prolonged periods of time as immune memory (Ahmed and Gray, 1996; Farber et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ahmed and Gray, 1996 and Farber et al., 2014.

claim: A fraction of expanded cells is retained over prolonged periods of time as immune memory.
source: Clonal selection expands the number of specific cells during an infection for effector functions, a fraction of which is retained over prolonged periods of time as immune memory (Ahmed and Gray, 1996; Farber et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ahmed and Gray, 1996 and Farber et al., 2014.

claim: Clone size distributions in two large cohort studies display a power-law relationship between the rank and size of the largest clones.
source: (B, C) Clone size distributions in two large cohort studies of human blood samples using disparate sequencing protocols display a power-law relationship between the rank and size of the largest clones.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and 1C from two cohort studies (Britanova et al., 2016 and Emerson et al., 2017).

claim: Power-law exponents fitted from the Britanova cohort are α = 1.17 ± 0.03 (mean ± standard error).
source: Determined in this subsampling-robust manner the fitted power-law exponents agree remarkably well within the range of ages covered by both cohorts (Figure 1D): with α = 1.17 ± 0.03 (mean ± standard error [SE]) and α = 1.18 ± 0.01 in the Britanova cohort and Emerson cohort, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data from the Britanova cohort.

claim: Power-law exponents fitted from the Emerson cohort are α = 1.18 ± 0.01.
source: Determined in this subsampling-robust manner the fitted power-law exponents agree remarkably well within the range of ages covered by both cohorts (Figure 1D): with α = 1.17 ± 0.03 (mean ± standard error [SE]) and α = 1.18 ± 0.01 in the Britanova cohort and Emerson cohort, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data from the Emerson cohort.

claim: The fitted power-law exponents varied little between individuals in both cohorts.
source: Moreover, the fitted exponents varied little between individuals in both cohorts; with a sample standard deviation of fitted exponents of 0.14 and 0.21, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing low standard deviations in fitted exponents.

claim: Repertoire formation is driven by increased thymic output and large proliferative expansion of some T cell clones in mice.
source: Our hypothesis is based on experimental evidence in mice (Le Campion et al., 2002; Min et al., 2003; Haluszczak et al., 2009; Kawabe et al., 2017) and human (Rufer et al., 1999; Schönland et al., 2003) that repertoire formation is driven not only by increased thymic output, but also by large proliferative expansion of some T cell clones.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies in mice.

claim: Repertoire formation is driven by increased thymic output and large proliferative expansion of some T cell clones in humans.
source: Our hypothesis is based on experimental evidence in mice (Le Campion et al., 2002; Min et al., 2003; Haluszczak et al., 2009; Kawabe et al., 2017) and human (Rufer et al., 1999; Schönland et al., 2003) that repertoire formation is driven not only by increased thymic output, but also by large proliferative expansion of some T cell clones.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in humans (Rufer et al., 1999; Schönland et al., 2003).

claim: Some T cell clones can persist over multiple decades.
source: Additionally, multiple studies Hammarlund et al., 2003; Pogorelyy et al., 2017; Tanno et al., 2020 have shown that some T cell clones can persist over multiple decades
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Hammarlund et al., 2003; Pogorelyy et al., 2017; Tanno et al., 2020).

claim: T cells proliferate at a rate inversely proportional to the total number of cells N already present in the repertoire.
source: Following previous work (Bains et al., 2009; Lythe et al., 2016), we assume that T cells proliferate at a rate inversely proportional to the total number of cells N already present in the repertoire.
evidence: This assumption is based on previous modeling work cited (Bains et al., 2009; Lythe et al., 2016).

claim: There is experimental evidence for increased proliferation early in life before the repertoire has reached its homeostatic size.
source: This assumption leads to increased proliferation early in life before the repertoire has reached its homeostatic size, for which there is experimental evidence Le Campion et al., 2002; Min et al., 2003; Haluszczak et al., 2009; Kawabe et al., 2017; Rufer et al., 1999; Schönland et al., 2003.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple experimental studies.

claim: The fraction of cells with TCR excision circles is constant during fetal development.
source: Importantly, recruitment of new clones and total expansion of already existing clones maintain a constant ratio throughout development under these assumptions in line with findings that the fraction of cells with TCR excision circles, which are diluted during peripheral division, is constant during fetal development (Schönland et al., 2003) and infancy (Douek et al., 2001; Bains et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schönland et al., 2003.

claim: The fraction of cells with TCR excision circles is constant during infancy.
source: Importantly, recruitment of new clones and total expansion of already existing clones maintain a constant ratio throughout development under these assumptions in line with findings that the fraction of cells with TCR excision circles, which are diluted during peripheral division, is constant during fetal development (Schönland et al., 2003) and infancy (Douek et al., 2001; Bains et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Douek et al., 2001 and Bains et al., 2009.

claim: Simulated repertoires at 5 years of age display power-law scaling of clone sizes.
source: We simulated the model starting from an empty repertoire and found that large clones displayed power-law scaling (Figure 2B blue lines).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The power-law tail persisted over multiple decades of aging in simulations.
source: The power-law tail persisted over multiple decades of aging, much beyond the timescale of cellular turnover, 1/d = 5 years, assumed in the simulations.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: The predicted exponent closely matches simulation results for different values of γ.
source: The predicted exponent closely matches simulation results for different values of γ (Figure 2D dashed lines).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of theoretical predictions with simulation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The enzyme terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is not expressed until the mid second trimester.
source: While T cells are produced by the thymus from the late first trimester the enzyme terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT), which inserts non-templated nucleotides during VDJ recombination, is not expressed until the mid second trimester (Park et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Park et al., 2020.

claim: Many more T cells in fetal and neonatal blood have zero insertions than expected from the adult recombination statistics.
source: Therefore, many more T cells in fetal and neonatal blood have zero insertions than expected from the adult recombination statistics (Rechavi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rechavi et al., 2015.

claim: Zero insertion clones are highly enriched within the most abundant clones.
source: Analyzing data from the Emerson cohort, we find that zero insertion clones are indeed highly enriched within the most abundant clones (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of data from the Emerson cohort shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Enrichment of zero insertion clones is particularly pronounced in the young and decreases with age at different speeds depending on clone size.
source: We find that enrichment is particularly pronounced in the young and decreases with age at different speeds depending on clone size.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Among the largest clones many more still have zero insertions than expected from the adult recombination statistics even multiple decades after repertoire formation.
source: Among the largest clones many more still have zero insertions than expected from the adult recombination statistics even multiple decades after repertoire formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Incumbent large clones created during repertoire formation are only slowly replaced by clones expanding later in life.
source: This suggests that the incumbent large clones created during repertoire formation are only slowly replaced by clones expanding later in life, similarly to what has been observed in mice (Gossel et al., 2017; Hogan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data on zero insertion enrichment and supported by citations to mouse studies (Gossel et al., 2017; Hogan et al., 2019).

claim: Sequences with zero insertions are similarly enriched among the largest clones in productive and unproductive sequences.
source: First, sequences with zero insertions are similarly enriched among the largest clones in productive and unproductive sequences (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) demonstrating that convergent selection pressures during adult life are not a primary source of the higher abundance of these clones.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Abundant clones are enriched for sequences with known antigen specificity.
source: Second, while abundant clones are also enriched for sequences with known antigen specificity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and sequences likely to be convergently recombined (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), these enrichments do not show the same striking dependence on age.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Zero insertion clones are consistently less enriched in individuals infected by CMV.
source: Furthermore, we find that zero insertion clones are consistently less enriched in individuals infected by CMV (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), in contrast to the hypothesis that this infection might drive their expansion (Pogorelyy et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Only a small fraction of the largest clones in any sample were not already large at the earliest time point in longitudinal data.
source: We first analyzed how much recently expanded clones contribute to the tail of the clone sizes, and found that only a small fraction of the largest clones in any sample were not already large at the earliest time point (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of longitudinal data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Large clones had remarkably stable abundances over time in longitudinal data.
source: We found that large clones had remarkably stable abundances over time, which we quantified by calculating the variance of log-foldchanges in clone size between the second and every subsequent time point (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of longitudinal data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The enrichment of zero insertion clones in the simulated cohort closely recapitulated the empirical findings using plausible parameter values.
source: The enrichment of zero insertion clones in the simulated cohort (Figure 4C) closely recapitulated the empirical findings using plausible parameter values.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results (Figure 4C) with empirical data.

claim: The timescales over which the enrichment decays agree remarkably well between simulated and empirical data.
source: Notably, the longer lasting enrichment of zero insertion clones among the very largest clones is also found in the simulated cohort, and the timescales over which the enrichment decays agree remarkably well.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with empirical data.

claim: The fitted characteristic timescale τd is approximately a decade.
source: In line with the long-lived enrichment of zero insertion clones, the fitting reveals a remarkably slow timescale of about a decade over which the clone size hierarchy is reordered during healthy aging.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitting the theoretical model to empirical data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Clonal expansions during a perinatal time window leave a long-lasting imprint on the human T cell repertoire.
source: We find that clonal expansions during a perinatal time window leave a long-lasting imprint on the human T cell repertoire, which is only slowly reshaped by fluctuating clonal selection during adult life.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple lines of evidence including zero insertion enrichment analysis and longitudinal dynamics.

claim: The T cell repertoire is remarkably stable over time in adult individuals outside of the punctuated expansions and contractions of specific clones in acute responses.
source: Notably, we find that the T cell repertoire is remarkably stable over time in adult individuals outside of the punctuated expansions and contractions of specific clones in acute responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal data analysis showing stable clone sizes over time.

claim: Early pathogen exposures are particularly potent in shaping the immune repertoire.
source: We thus expect early pathogen exposures to be particularly potent, as has been observed in influenza, where disease severity across age cohorts for different strains depends on the first exposure (Gostic et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gostic et al., 2016 and is consistent with the model predictions.

claim: The presence of tolerizing factors early in life is particularly crucial during repertoire formation to avoid autoimmunity.
source: Conversely, we expect the presence of tolerizing factors early in life to be particularly crucial during repertoire formation to avoid autoimmunity, as has been observed for the autoimmune regulator gene AIRE, for which expression is only essential during a perinatal time window (Guerau-de-Arellano et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guerau-de-Arellano et al., 2009 and is consistent with the model predictions.

claim: The largest clones predominantly consist of cells with memory phenotype.
source: Repertoire sequencing of phenotypically sorted blood samples shows that the largest clones predominantly consist of cells with memory phenotype (Appendix 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of phenotypically sorted samples discussed in Appendix 5.

claim: A substantial number of memory cells circulate in the blood quickly following birth.
source: Supporting this interpretation, a substantial number of memory cells circulate in the blood quickly following birth (Pediatric AIDS Clinical Trials Group et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pediatric AIDS Clinical Trials Group et al., 2003.

claim: Memory-like T cells are already generated in particular tissue sites such as the intestine even before birth.
source: and recent evidence suggests that memory-like T cells are already generated in particular tissue sites such as the intestine even before birth (Zhang et al., 2014; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2014 and Li et al., 2019.

claim: The Britanova cohort comprises 71 individuals spanning ages 6–103 years, as well as eight cord blood samples.
source: The Britanova cohort comprises 71 individuals spanning ages 6–103 years, as well as eight cord blood samples.
evidence: This is a description of the data source used in the study.

claim: The Emerson cohort spans ages 1–74 years and consists of a training and validation set of 666 and 120 individuals, respectively.
source: The Emerson cohort spans ages 1–74 years and consists of a training and validation set of 666 and 120 individuals, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of the data source used in the study.

claim: Chronic infection with CMV drives large clonal expansions.
source: Chronic infection with CMV drives large clonal expansions (Lindau et al., 2019; Sylwester et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lindau et al., 2019 and Sylwester et al., 2005.

claim: CMV-positive individuals have a smaller α than uninfected individuals.
source: Overall, CMV-positive individuals have a smaller α than uninfected individuals, which is independent of age.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The average exponent in CMV-negative individuals decreases slowly with age.
source: The average exponent in CMV-negative individuals decreases slowly with age, and in old age coincides those of CMV-positive individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Men have on average a slightly smaller exponent than women indicating a more skewed repertoire organization.
source: We find that the dependence on age is similar among the sexes, but men have on average a slightly smaller exponent than women indicating a more skewed repertoire organization.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The naive cell fraction as determined by flow cytometry and the fraction of singletons are closely correlated in the Britanova cohort.
source: (A) The naive cell fraction as determined by flow cytometry and the fraction of singletons are closely correlated in the Britanova cohort.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Filtering naive clones that are also found in the memory compartment removes most large naive clones.
source: Filtering naive clones that are also found in the memory compartment removes most large naive clones.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Frequency of large clones in the memory sample is shifted upwards relative to their frequency within the unsorted sample.
source: (C) Frequency of large clones in the memory sample is shifted upwards relative to their frequency within the unsorted sample.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The fraction of naive cells decreases with age starting in early infancy.
source: (D) The fraction of naive cells decreases with age (Data source: Britanova et al., 2016) starting in early infancy (Data source: Pediatric AIDS Clinical Trials Group et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Britanova et al., 2016 and Pediatric AIDS Clinical Trials Group et al., 2003 shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The fitted power-law exponents α = 2.1 ± 0.1 (mean ± SE) in cord blood samples are larger than in adult repertoires.
source: The fitted power-law exponents α = 2.1 ± 0.1 (mean ± SE) are larger than in adult repertoires, but clone sizes are already remarkably broad.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of cord blood samples shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Clone sizes are already remarkably broad at birth.
source: The fitted power-law exponents α = 2.1 ± 0.1 (mean ± SE) are larger than in adult repertoires, but clone sizes are already remarkably broad.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of cord blood samples shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Power-law scaling of clone sizes spanning several orders of magnitude has been observed in multiple studies.
source: A particularly striking such pattern has been the observation of power-law scaling of clone sizes spanning several orders of magnitude (Robins et al., 2009; Thomas et al., 2014; Britanova et al., 2016; Emerson et al., 2017; Oakes et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Power-law scaling of clone sizes has been shown to arise at steady state in models of fluctuating clonal selection driven by different antigen encounters.
source: Such power-law scaling of clone sizes has been shown to arise at steady state in models of fluctuating clonal selection driven by different antigen encounters (Desponds et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Desponds et al., 2016.

claim: Lifetimes of several years and several months have been measured by deuterium labeling for naive and memory T cells, respectively.
source: Lifetimes of several years and several months have been measured by deuterium labeling for naive and memory T cells, respectively (De Boer and Perelson, 2013; Borghans et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to De Boer and Perelson, 2013 and Borghans et al., 2018.

claim: T cell memory has been observed to decline with half-lives of 8–15 years by following titers after small pox vaccination.
source: For example, T cell memory has been observed to decline with half-lives of 8–15 years by following titers after small pox vaccination (Hammarlund et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hammarlund et al., 2003.

claim: Two studies of identical twins have shown an excess sharing of identical clones decades after in utero blood exchange in monochorionic twins.
source: Another line of direct evidence for long clonal persistence has come from two studies of identical twins (Pogorelyy et al., 2017; Tanno et al., 2020), which have shown an excess sharing of identical clones decades after in utero blood exchange in monochorionic twins.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pogorelyy et al., 2017 and Tanno et al., 2020.
